idiom_name: promise (write end) + future (read end) over a once-only shared state
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: the producer keeps a single-assignment container (promise/resolver) and hands the consumer a read-only handle (future/awaitable); both refer to the same shared state. The producer computes out of band and makes the state ready with a value or a failure, the consumer tests readiness, waits or registers a continuation, and the runtime (event loop, thread pool, coroutine scheduler) resumes the continuation once the state is ready. Resolution must be idempotent and total - every exit path, including exceptions, has to make the state ready - publication of the result is part of the contract rather than the user's job, and composition (map/all/any/select, timeouts, cancellation) is expressed as operations on handles that do not block.
code_sketch:
p = promise()                     # write end (single assignment)
f = p.future                      # read end handed to the caller
spawn { p.fulfil(compute()) }     # or p.fail(err) on every exit path

v = await f                       # read end: suspends, does not block a thread
# also: f.then(handle, report) | f.join(timeout) | combine(f, g) | f.cancel()
pitfalls: An operation whose outcome nobody collects: values and failures disappear silently.
Blocking inside the runtime that must complete the handle (event loop, single-thread pool, dispatcher): deadlock or starvation.
Unbounded task creation: the pattern bounds nothing by itself, so overload moves into queues and memory unless the executor is limited.
Settling the state twice, or never on an error path: waiters either see a stale outcome or hang forever.
Cancellation, deadline and ambient context not propagated into the operation or back out of the continuation.

Handler accumulation on long-lived handles: race/any/select subscribe to every input and promise-style handles offer no unsubscribe, so repeatedly racing a never-settling promise accumulates handlers and retains every co-raced result — a conformance-legal leak that ends in OOM in long-running processes (nodejs/node#51452).

Watchdog timers outlive their operation: a timeout promise built from a timer keeps the timer, and everything its closure captured, alive until it fires even when the operation finished; clear it in finally or use the platform timeout signal, otherwise every call leaks one timer plus payload under load.

Settlement is observable only in a later turn: handlers run as microtasks, so resolved does not mean visible in this tick; a handler attached after rejection bookkeeping has already run can arrive too late, and the stack reported points into library plumbing rather than at the origin of the failure.
Microtask starvation: a loop that awaits already-settled promises never yields to the timer and IO phase, so timers, IO and rendering stall while the code still looks like ordinary async code.

Cancellation cannot be told apart from failure: AbortError, TimeoutError, CancelledError and Swift's boolean-only cancellation all arrive as errors to a generic handler, so client-went-away and deadline-exceeded collapse into one alarm unless the reason is captured and carried.

Cooperative cancellation stops nothing by itself: tokens and boolean flags only work where the work checks them; spawned or detached work may be unstoppable, and drop-based cancellation only takes effect at the next await point.

Cancellation is not rollback: dropping a handle discards the computation wherever it happens to be suspended, so a half-applied write, a consumed message, an open transaction or an already-charged side effect can be left behind — cancellation points must sit where the state is consistent.

Unobserved-outcome detection is deferred and opportunistic: .NET raises the unobserved-task event only when a faulted task is finalized, Python's never-retrieved-exception warning appears only in debug mode, and a settled handle parked in an in-flight map keeps its exception, stack trace and captured context alive indefinitely.

Lazy and eager hide under one name: an unawaited Rust future never runs at all while a spawned task runs even when its handle is dropped; C++ deferred async runs on the first wait in the waiting thread while an abandoned async future may block at scope exit — the same mistake has opposite consequences in different runtimes.

Deadlines that only settle the handle: orTimeout, completeOnTimeout and race-based timeouts complete the future without stopping the operation, so the timed-out request keeps a connection, a thread and a downstream slot busy — the work needs its own cancellation channel.

Structured-scope escapes: CancellationToken.None, context.Background(), fresh GlobalScope or ad-hoc detached task disconnects inner work from the caller's lifetime, so the work outlives the request and its failure reaches nobody.

Composition hides partial failure: join and allOf report one aggregate failure with no per-item results unless the inputs were retained, Promise.all discards every sibling result at the first rejection, and asyncio.gather leaves remaining tasks running after the first exception — error handling written for the happy shape silently drops work.

One handle, several waiters: implementations differ on whether the value reaches every waiter or is consumed by the first, so sharing a single-consumption handle between consumers loses outcomes or double-counts work.

Promises are eager while Futures are often lazy: a promise starts executing at construction while a future may not run until it is awaited — mixing the two semantics in the same codebase creates invisible divergences where one pattern works and the other hangs.

Wrong move: call get(), join() or result() on the event-loop or single-thread executor -> the worker that must complete the future is blocked and progress deadlocks or starves -> instead await it or move blocking work to a separate bounded executor.

Wrong move: race a future against a timeout and treat timeout completion as cancellation -> the underlying operation keeps consuming its thread, connection or downstream slot -> instead propagate a cancellation signal or deadline to the operation and clean up the timer in finally.

Wrong move: start a future and drop its handle -> failure has no owner and may surface only as an unhandled rejection or never-retrieved exception -> instead await or join it, attach terminal error handling, or mark deliberate detachment with an explicit supervisor.
